stem: If \(|\vec{a}| = 2\), \(|\vec{b}| = 3\), \(|\vec{c}| = 4\) then \(\left[\ \vec{a}+\vec{b}\ \ \ \vec{b}+\vec{c}\ \ \ \vec{c}-\vec{a}\ \right]\) is equal to
solution: Expand \([\vec{a}+\vec{b},\ \vec{b}+\vec{c},\ \vec{c}-\vec{a}]\) using multilinearity of the scalar triple product. Term by term: \([\vec{a},\vec{b}+\vec{c},\vec{c}-\vec{a}] = [\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]\) (all other terms vanish due to repeated vectors), and \([\vec{b},\vec{b}+\vec{c},\vec{c}-\vec{a}] = -[\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{a}] = -[\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]\) (cyclic property). Adding: \([\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}] - [\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}] = 0\), independent of the given magnitudes.

stem: If \(|\vec{a}| = 3\), \(|\vec{b}| = 4\), then the value of \(\lambda\) for which \(\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{b}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b}\), is
solution: Perpendicularity gives \((\vec{a}+\lambda\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a}-\lambda\vec{b})=0 \Rightarrow |\vec{a}|^2-\lambda^2|\vec{b}|^2=0 \Rightarrow 9-16\lambda^2=0 \Rightarrow \lambda^2=\dfrac{9}{16} \Rightarrow \lambda=\dfrac{3}{4}\).

stem: If sum of two unit vectors is itself a unit vector, then the magnitude of their difference is
solution: \(|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2=1 \Rightarrow 1+1+2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=1 \Rightarrow \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\). Then \(|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2=1+1-2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=2+1=3 \Rightarrow |\vec{a}-\vec{b}|=\sqrt{3}\).

stem: If \(|\vec{a}| = 3\), \(|\vec{b}| = 5\), \(|\vec{c}| = 7\) and \(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=\vec{0}\), then the angle between \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) is
solution: [Textbook misprint: options B and C are both printed as \(\pi/4\).] Since \(\vec{c}=-(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\), \(|\vec{c}|^2=|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2+2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} \Rightarrow 49=9+25+2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} \Rightarrow \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=7.5\). So \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{7.5}{3\times5}=\dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}=60^\circ\). The correct value \(\pi/3\) is not distinctly printed (the intended option, likely at position C, is duplicated as \(\pi/4\) instead); the nearest slot is marked C here.

stem: The volume of tetrahedron whose vertices are \((1,-6,10)\), \((-1,-3,7)\), \((5,-1,\lambda)\) and \((7,-4,7)\) is 11 cu. units then the value of \(\lambda\) is
solution: [Textbook note: option B \(\pi/3\) is not a meaningful choice for this coordinate/volume problem — an apparent carry-over misprint from a neighboring angle question.] Taking the first vertex as origin, edge vectors are \((-2,3,-3)\), \((4,5,\lambda-10)\), \((6,2,-3)\). Their scalar triple product works out to \(22\lambda-88\), so Volume \(=\dfrac{1}{6}|22\lambda-88|=11 \Rightarrow |22\lambda-88|=66\), giving \(\lambda=7\) or \(\lambda=1\); both satisfy the equation algebraically (both appear among the options, A and C) — 7 is taken as the primary intended value.

solution: \(\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1 \Rightarrow 0.25+0.5+\cos^2\gamma=1 \Rightarrow \cos^2\gamma=0.25 \Rightarrow \cos\gamma=\pm0.5 \Rightarrow \gamma=60^\circ\text{ or }120^\circ\).

solution: Distance from the Y-axis \(=\sqrt{x^2+z^2}=\sqrt{9+25}=\sqrt{34}\).

stem: The line joining the points \((-2, 1, -8)\) and \((a, b, c)\) is parallel to the line whose direction ratios are 6, 2, 3. The value of a, b, c are
solution: The direction ratios of the joining line are \((a+2, b-1, c+8)\), which should be exactly \((6,2,3)\): \(a+2=6, b-1=2, c+8=3 \Rightarrow a=4, b=3, c=-5\).

stem: If \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\) are the direction cosines of a line then the value of \(\sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma\) is
solution: \(\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma = 3-(\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma) = 3-1=2\).

solution: By definition, \(l,m,n\) are the direction cosines, so \(l\hat{i}+m\hat{j}+n\hat{k}\) has magnitude \(\sqrt{l^2+m^2+n^2}=1\) and lies along the line — the unit vector along the line.

stem: If \(|\vec{a}| = 3\) and \(-1 \le k \le 2\), then \(|k\vec{a}|\) lies in the interval

stem: Let \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) be distinct real numbers. The points with position vectors \(\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}\), \(\beta\hat{i}+\gamma\hat{j}+\alpha\hat{k}\), \(\gamma\hat{i}+\alpha\hat{j}+\beta\hat{k}\)
solution: Each pairwise squared distance simplifies to \(2(\alpha-\beta)^2+2(\beta-\gamma)^2+2(\gamma-\alpha)^2\) divided symmetrically — a direct computation shows all three side lengths are equal, so the three points form an equilateral triangle.

stem: Let \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\) be the position vectors of P and Q respectively, with respect to O and \(|\vec{p}| = p\), \(|\vec{q}| = q\). The points R and S divide PQ internally and externally in the ratio 2 : 3 respectively. If OR and OS are perpendicular then.
solution: \(\vec{r}=\dfrac{3\vec{p}+2\vec{q}}{5}\) (internal 2:3) and \(\vec{s}=3\vec{p}-2\vec{q}\) (external 2:3). \(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{s}=0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{5}\left(9|\vec{p}|^2-4|\vec{q}|^2\right)=0 \Rightarrow 9p^2=4q^2\) (the cross terms cancel).

stem: The 2 vectors \(\hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\) represents the two sides AB and AC, respectively of a \(\triangle ABC\). The length of the median through A is
solution: Taking A as origin, midpoint of BC is \(\dfrac{(\hat{j}+\hat{k})+(3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+4\hat{k})}{2}=\dfrac{3\hat{i}+5\hat{k}}{2}\). Length of median \(=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^2+\left(\tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{34}{4}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{34}}{2}\).

stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are unit vectors, then what is the angle between \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) for \(\sqrt{3}\vec{a} - \vec{b}\) to be a unit vector?
solution: \(|\sqrt{3}\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2=1 \Rightarrow 3+1-2\sqrt{3}\cos\theta=1 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=30^\circ\).

solution: \(|\vec{a}||\vec{b}||\cos\theta| = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}||\sin\theta| \Rightarrow |\tan\theta|=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

stem: The value of \(\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k}) + \hat{j}\cdot(\hat{i}\times\hat{k}) + \hat{k}\cdot(\hat{i}\times\hat{j})\)
solution: \(\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i} \Rightarrow \hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1\); \(\hat{i}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{j} \Rightarrow \hat{j}\cdot(-\hat{j})=-1\); \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k} \Rightarrow \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1\). Sum \(=1-1+1=1\).

stem: Let a, b, c be distinct non-negative numbers. If the vectors \(a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}+c\hat{k}\), \(\hat{i}+\hat{k}\) and \(c\hat{i}+c\hat{j}+b\hat{k}\) lie in a plane, then c is

options.label: A
options.text: The arithmetic mean of a and b

options.label: B
options.text: The geometric mean of a and b

options.label: C

solution: Coplanarity gives \(\begin{vmatrix}a & a & c\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ c & c & b\end{vmatrix}=0 \Rightarrow -ab+c^2=0 \Rightarrow c^2=ab \Rightarrow c=\sqrt{ab}\), the geometric mean of a and b.

stem: Let \(\vec{a} = \hat{i}-\hat{j}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{j}-\hat{k}\), \(\vec{c} = \hat{k}-\hat{i}\). If \(\vec{d}\) is a unit vector such that \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d}=0=[\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]\), then \(\vec{d}\) equals.
solution: \([\vec{b}\ \vec{c}\ \vec{d}]=0\) means \(\vec{d}\) is coplanar with \(\vec{b},\vec{c}\), so \(\vec{d}=\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c}=(-\gamma,\beta,\gamma-\beta)\). \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{d}=0\) gives \(-\gamma-\beta=0 \Rightarrow \beta=-\gamma\), so \(\vec{d}=\gamma(-1,-1,2)\). Normalizing: \(|\gamma|\sqrt{6}=1\), giving \(\vec{d}=\pm\dfrac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}}\).

stem: If \(\vec{a}\ \vec{b}\ \vec{c}\) are non coplanar unit vectors such that \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) = \dfrac{(\vec{b}+\vec{c})}{\sqrt{2}}\) then the angle between \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) is
solution: Using \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\vec{b}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\vec{b}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\vec{c}\). Since \(\vec{b},\vec{c}\) are independent, \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(-\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). As unit vectors, \(\cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).
